unknowns: Opcode semantics above `0x7F` (`0x90`, `0x91`, `0x93`, `0xb1`, …): the bodies use operators the note's token table does not list, and this audit does not name them.  They are decoded only as parm-list operators, and only where the nesting balances exactly; which of `0x90`/`0x91` is multiply and which is divide is not established here.  A runnable oracle (the game's VM) is outside the read-only inputs.

The trailer's own fields (the bytes before the FName): neither the note nor this audit identifies them.  Only the length, the constant tail (FName index + 0) and the effect on the body boundary are decoded.
The 145 exports with a 17-byte trailer are counted, not explained.
`Next`/`SuperField` are checked for resolution and class, not by walking the UField chain in order.
verdict: STRUCTURE HOLDS; BODY LENGTH IS ONE BYTE SHORT
verdict_points: Head offsets 0/2/6/10/14/18: **confirmed**, each by an oracle over all 29620 `Function` exports (`u16@0` zero 29620/29620, `Children` an own property 22737/29620, trailing FName = own name 29620/29620).

Body length: **one byte wrong**.  `ScriptSize` is the number of body bytes, not `len + 1`; the note's `len(export) - 38` cuts the last byte in 29475 of 29620 exports (and keeps one trailer byte in 145).  A token scan of ScriptSize bytes ends exactly on the last byte in 26039 bodies against 14456 for the note's length.
Trailer: 15 bytes, 17 on 145 exports, always ending in the own FName + a zero number; the note's `flags word @size-16` is not a field and `pre-name word == 0x0002xxxx` is not exact.

Anchors: 5 of the note's 7 hold as stated (A_super, A_children, D_name, E_native_parm_refs — 3407/3407 refs over 1825 stubs — and F_call_token at 54022/54211); 2 do not (B_script_size_is_len_plus_one, C_thinnest_script_is_return).

Constants: every literal the note quotes for the three audited functions re-decodes to the quoted value, and no plausible float in those bodies is unaccounted for; the note quotes no offsets, this audit adds them.

Rules: §3.1's armour-mode reduction and §3.4's unconditional `return true` both trace to exact bytecode; §3.4 is also the case where the one-byte error bites, because the cut byte is what completes `return ReturnValue`.
